newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysian firms go abroad on asset buying spree.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysian firms go abroad on asset buying spree.

text.p: Flush with cash and hungry for new markets, Malaysian corporations have gone on a spree to acquire quality-enhancing assets in developed countries.

Although Malaysian companies have made scores of acquisitions and joint ventures in Asia's emerging markets, it is only lately that they have focused their energies on countries that not too long ago were more accustomed to being the purchasers.
"We've gone through a period in the last six years, where a lot of multinationals have been poking around in Malaysia," said Razani Radzi, head of research at PB Securities.
"Malaysians are seeing that the services provided by these multinationals can be owned by Malaysians," he said.

In a regular New Sunday Times column on November 3, its group editor Abdul Kadir Jasin said companies operating abroad should report regularly on the progress of their investments and the profits they are bringing home, to allow the public to judge the benefits of overseas ventures.

"They will only be convinced of the benefits of this policy when profits and new technology start to flow into the country in a big way. As it stands, not much is known about the progress of these projects and even less about the profits that are being repatriated," Abdul Kadir said.
Just last week, one cross-country deal was sealed, while another widely-speculated acquisition unravelled.

National carmaker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton) and its chairman said last Wednesday they had jointly bought an 80 percent stake in Group Lotus Ltd, a maker of sports cars and provider of auto engineering services.

In paying $82 million for the stake, they beat South Korea's Daewoo Motor Co Ltd, a unit of Daewoo group. And then there was the YTL Corp Bhd deal, which also came to light. The infrastructure developer and power concern said on Tuesday it had decided to withdraw a $2.6 billion bid to buy a 60 percent stake in Hong Kong power firm Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA).

YTL, with the backing of the Malaysian government's investment arm, had been bidding against U.S. utility firm Southern Co, which had already agreed to buy most of the stake from CEPA parent Hopewell Holdings Ltd for about $2.7 billion.
HONG KONG AND BRITAIN IN OTHER DEALS
Hong Kong and Britain have featured in other Malaysian deals this year.
Hauler and shipper Konsortium Perkapalan Bhd in July acquired U.S.-listed, Hong Kong-based Pacific Basin Bulk Shipping Ltd for $230 million in a deal which boosted its fleet and regional presence.

The same month, infrastructure firm Intria Bhd purchased a 40 percent stake in U.K. builder Costain Group Plc for 159 million ringgit ($64 million), giving it more expertise for overseas job bids, analysts said.
In May, plantations concern Kuala Lumpur Kepong Bhd signed a pact to buy the toiletries company Crabtree & Evelyn Ltd for $60 million in cash as part of a business diversification.
The theme in the deals has been one of technical and technology transfer, analysts said.

"The Proton interest in Lotus had to do with buying expertise," said an equity analyst with a local brokerage firm. "They're willing to pay a premium for that. They can transfer the knowledge back to their own operations."
Malaysia's government, keen to elevate an economy that was once heavily commodities-based, has encouraged corporations to go into value-added, high-technology businesses.
And, with a population of over 21 million experiencing the ninth year of over eight percent economic growth, Malaysian companies are finding the domestic market too small for their ambitions.

"It's the natural evolution of an economy," said Richard Jones, head of research at ING Barings. "Once the domestic base gets so high, naturally, you look overseas to diversify. It's a country's notion of portfolio management.
"Now, companies have the financial resources, and the strength to fund it."
FOLLOWING JAPAN, SINGAPORE'S LEAD
Singapore and Japan took similar paths in the past, analysts noted.
Like Japan, Malaysia's government is assuming a leading role in the corporate expansions, which have evolved from a Malaysia Incorporated Policy launched in 1983, analysts said.
The policy, which included privatisations of large government corporations, aimed to develop all aspects of Malaysia through the model of a company.
"This (overseas asset buying) is an advanced version of that to create a more corporatised Malaysia where there is a higher level of efficiency," said Razani at PB Securities.
Judging from government officials' comments, more acquisitions are expected, analysts said. Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad spoke ruefully of the aborted YTL bid "as a good deal that got away".
He also sharply defended the decision by state investment arm Khazanah Nasional Bhd, to provide a $1 billion loan for the deal. "We're not as stupid as we're thought to be," he said.
An equities salesman in a Hong Kong brokerage said: "People who don't know the country remain sceptical (about the acquisitions).
"(But) this is not just a public relations exercise. Malaysian companies do have quite a lot of cash, and they need to upgrade their technology. It makes a lot of sense." ($1 =2.5 ringgit)
